messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Actor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 66

# The Weight of the Stage

Karim is a fifty-two-year-old Lebanese-born actor who has spent the better part of three decades building a quiet but respected career in theater and television. He carries himself with the practiced ease of someone accustomed to inhabiting other people's lives — a quality that, until three years ago, felt like a gift. Now it feels like a trap.

Three years ago, Karim's wife of twenty-one years, Nadia, was struck by a car while crossing the street outside their apartment building. He was standing on the sidewalk no more than ten feet away, having just stepped ahead of her to hail a cab. He heard the impact before he saw it. He turned and watched her fall. He ran to her, knelt beside her on the asphalt, and held her hand while strangers called for help. She died in the hospital four hours later without regaining consciousness. Karim sat alone in a waiting room chair, still wearing the coat he had put on to take her to dinner for their anniversary.

In the weeks that followed, Karim moved through the rituals of grief — the funeral, the condolences, the quiet apartment — in a state of numbness that he initially mistook for resilience. He returned to work within a month, telling himself that Nadia would have wanted him to. But something had changed in his relationship to performance. Where he had once been able to disappear into a character, he now found himself ambushed by sensation. During a stage production that autumn, a scene involving a car horn sent him stumbling backward into the wings, his chest locked, his vision narrowing to a pinhole. He told the director he had stumbled on a prop.

He has not told anyone what actually happened.

Karim rarely sleeps past three in the morning. He wakes with the sound of the impact still fresh in his ears — not remembered so much as replayed, as though his mind has no interest in the distinction between then and now. He lies in the dark and goes over the geometry of that moment obsessively: if he had walked more slowly, if he had let her go first, if he had chosen a different restaurant. The calculations never resolve. They simply begin again.

During the day, he avoids the block where it happened, adding twelve minutes to every commute without acknowledging why. He has quietly declined two roles that required him to portray grief or loss, citing scheduling conflicts. He sits with his back to windows when he can. He flinches at the sound of tires on wet pavement. These adjustments have become so automatic that he rarely registers them as choices anymore — they are simply the shape his days have taken.

What troubles Karim most, and what he speaks about with the halting precision of a man choosing each word carefully, is the feeling that he is no longer entirely present in his own life. He can deliver a monologue with technical precision, can make an audience weep, and then walk offstage and feel absolutely nothing. He describes it as being very good at pretending to be alive. He is aware of the irony. He does not find it funny.

He speaks of Nadia with a tenderness that is also a kind of torment. He keeps her photograph on the nightstand but sometimes turns it face-down before bed because looking at her feels unbearable and not looking feels like a betrayal. He has not removed her coat from the hook by the door. He has not allowed himself to cry in front of another person since the day she died, though he is uncertain whether this is strength or simply one more performance he cannot stop giving.

He came to therapy, he says, because a colleague mentioned it offhandedly, and because he had run out of ways to be convincing — to others, and increasingly, to himself.
